title: Data Quality and the Analysis Workflow
summary: Learn to check whether a dataset is fit for purpose using four quality checks (completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy), follow a six-stage repeatable analysis workflow, and apply basic data-ethics and privacy principles when handling and sharing data.

steps.title: Is the data any good?
steps.lede: Before drawing conclusions from the delivery-orders table, you need to ask one question first: is this data fit for the purpose?

blocks.text: Data quality means whether a dataset is fit for the purpose it will be used for — not whether it looks tidy, but whether it can actually support the question you're asking. Before trusting any conclusion drawn from the Kwik Courier delivery-orders table, you need to check whether the data itself is reliable enough to answer that question.

Two checks look at what is missing or repeated. Completeness checks whether the records and values that should be present actually are — for example, an order row with no delivery time recorded at all. Uniqueness checks whether a record that should appear only once is duplicated — for example, the same order number showing up as two separate rows.

segments.label: Data-quality dimensions explained one at a time: accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, uniqueness
segments.summary: Presents data quality dimensions as separate factors, each measuring one aspect of how suitable a dataset is for its intended purpose, and walks through them one by one. Accuracy means the data reflects real-life facts and is checked against trusted sources; completeness means the important details are all there; consistency means the same value agrees wherever it appears (a phone number with an international code in one system but not another); validity means values fit the required format or rules (a zip code with the right number of digits, a date in the right format); uniqueness means no duplicates, so one person is not billed twice. Stops before the next dimension, integrity.

segments.label: Data quality as fitness for purpose, shown on one phone-and-email marketing list
segments.summary: Describes data quality as keeping data useful for its intended business purpose, then runs one example, a spreadsheet of phone numbers and email addresses for a marketing campaign, through the checks. Accuracy: the contact details were recorded correctly. Completeness: no customer is missing a phone number or email. Validity: emails contain an @ symbol and phone numbers start with a country code. Uniqueness: no contact is repeated. Timeliness: year-old contact data would be useless. It also uses consistency to mean data moving between systems without being altered, for instance software adding a stray quotation mark to each email.

steps.title: Validity, accuracy, and good enough
steps.lede: Two more checks look at whether the values themselves are trustworthy — and data doesn't have to be perfect to be useful.

blocks.text: Validity checks whether a column's values are in the range and format expected — a delivery time of −5 minutes fails validity because negative time is not a valid delivery time. Accuracy checks whether the data correctly matches the real-world thing it describes — an order logged as delivered to Lagos when the driver actually delivered it to Abuja is complete, unique and validly formatted, but still inaccurate.

Good-quality data does not have to be perfect. The goal of these checks is not a flawless dataset; it is a dataset good enough to answer the question you actually have, using completeness, uniqueness, validity and accuracy as the specific things to look for.

steps.title: Fitness for purpose and missing or duplicate records
steps.lede: Apply what you've learned about completeness and uniqueness.

public.prompt: An analyst wants to use the Kwik Courier delivery-orders table to find the average delivery time per city. She notices that order 1003 appears as two identical rows. Which statement best describes the problem and whether the data is fit for this purpose?

options.text: The duplicate row is a uniqueness failure; the data is not fit for purpose until the duplicate is removed, because it would inflate the order count.
The duplicate row is a completeness failure; the data is fit for purpose because all values are present.
The duplicate row is a validity failure; the data is fit for purpose because the values are in the correct format.
There is no problem; having two rows for the same order is normal in a delivery table.

opt_s04_b.message: Completeness checks for missing values, not duplicates. A duplicate row is a uniqueness failure — one entity (one order) should appear as exactly one row.

opt_s04_c.message: Validity checks whether values are in the expected range or format. A duplicate row is a uniqueness failure, not a validity failure.

opt_s04_d.message: A record that should appear once appearing twice is a uniqueness failure. It would count the same order twice when calculating averages, making the data unfit for this purpose without correction.

correct.message: Correct. Uniqueness checks whether a record that should appear once is duplicated. A duplicate order row would inflate the order count and skew the average, so the data is not fit for purpose until the duplicate is removed.

incorrect.message: Not quite. Think about which check covers repeated records: completeness is about missing values, validity is about format and range, and uniqueness is about records that should appear only once.

hints: Which of the four checks is specifically about records that should appear only once?
Would counting order 1003 twice give you an accurate average delivery time per city?

steps.title: Invalid vs inaccurate values, and good-enough data
steps.lede: Distinguish validity failures from accuracy failures, and recognise when data is good enough.

public.prompt: Order 1006 has delivery_minutes = −5. In a hypothetical scenario, Order 1007 is logged as delivered to Lagos, but the driver's GPS shows the delivery was actually in Port Harcourt. Which row has a validity failure, which has an accuracy failure, and what does this mean for fitness for purpose?

options.text: Order 1006 has a validity failure (−5 is not a valid delivery time); order 1007 has an accuracy failure (wrong city). Neither makes the whole dataset unfit for purpose — the analyst should note both problems and decide whether they affect the specific question.
Order 1006 has an accuracy failure (the time is wrong); order 1007 has a validity failure (the city name is in the wrong format).
Both rows have validity failures because neither value matches the real world.
Both rows have accuracy failures because the data does not match what actually happened.

opt_s05_b.message: Validity checks whether a value is in the expected range or format — −5 minutes is outside the valid range for a delivery time, so order 1006 fails validity. Order 1007's city name 'Lagos' is a valid format; the problem is that it doesn't match reality, which is an accuracy failure.

opt_s05_c.message: Validity is about range and format, not about matching reality. −5 minutes fails validity (not a valid delivery time). 'Lagos' is a valid city name in the correct format — the problem with order 1007 is accuracy, not validity.

opt_s05_d.message: Accuracy checks whether data matches the real world. Order 1007 fails accuracy. But order 1006's problem is different: −5 minutes is not a valid delivery time regardless of what happened in reality — that is a validity failure.

correct.message: Correct. Validity is about range and format (−5 minutes is not a valid delivery time); accuracy is about matching reality (the wrong city is recorded). Good-quality data does not have to be perfect — the analyst notes the problems and judges whether they affect the specific question.

incorrect.message: Think about the difference: validity asks 'is this value in the expected range or format?', while accuracy asks 'does this value correctly match the real-world thing it describes?'

hints: Could −5 minutes ever be a valid delivery time, regardless of what actually happened?
Is 'Lagos' an invalid city name, or is the problem that it doesn't match where the delivery actually went?

steps.title: A repeatable order for analysis
steps.lede: Knowing what to check is only half the job — you also need to know what order to do things in.

blocks.text: A repeatable analysis process typically begins by clarifying the question or purpose — for the Kwik Courier data, that might be 'which cities have unusually slow deliveries?' Clarifying this first means both you and whoever asked for the analysis share an understanding of what is being analyzed and why, before any work starts.

Next comes inspecting and cleaning. Before analysis, the data should be inspected and checked for quality so problems are addressed early — this is where the completeness, uniqueness, validity and accuracy checks come in. Cleaning then helps reduce quality problems such as duplication and inconsistent values, for example removing the duplicate order row found during inspection.

segments.summary: Follows one real analysis, an employee engagement survey, through its stages. First ask what problem is being solved and what the stakeholders hope to learn. Then prepare: decide what kind of data is needed and whether it must be collected or already exists. Then clean, treated as a first look at the data's structure plus quality-assurance questions about missing data, correct coding and unusual values. Then analyze, running the analyses planned from the original questions while letting the data speak rather than confirming a hunch. Finally share the findings, starting with high-level results for the executive team.

blocks.group_title: One analysis from question to findings

steps.title: Analyzing and visualizing are different steps
steps.lede: Examining the data and turning it into a graphic are two distinct jobs — keeping them separate matters.

blocks.text: Analyzing means examining the prepared data to answer the question. Exploratory data analysis looks at the data to uncover its underlying structure and spot anomalies — unusual values, like one delivery that took far longer than every other in the batch. For the Kwik Courier data, analyzing might mean looking closely at the cleaned rows to see which cities' deliveries stand out.

Visualizing is its own step: turning data into plots or other graphics. Exploratory data analysis relies mostly on such graphical techniques to gain insight and reveal structure, but making the graphic is a different job from examining the data. For the delivery data, visualizing might mean turning those delivery times into a graphic so the pattern is easy to see at a glance.

steps.title: Communicating findings is part of the workflow
steps.lede: The analysis isn't done when the numbers are ready — sharing what they mean, and how far they can be trusted, is the final stage.

blocks.text: The final stage is communicating the findings, and how far they can be trusted, to the people who will use them — not merely producing the analysis itself. Telling a manager that Lagos deliveries are running slow but the sample is small is part of the workflow.

This process is commonly iterative rather than strictly linear. If analyzing the delivery data turns up a value that looks wrong, you go back and inspect or clean it before continuing — earlier stages may be revisited as later stages reveal new issues.

steps.title: The workflow loops back
steps.lede: Recognise when and why the process revisits earlier stages.

public.prompt: While analyzing the cleaned Kwik Courier delivery data, the analyst spots a delivery time of 480 minutes — far higher than any other order. She suspects it was logged incorrectly. What should she do next, and why does this show the workflow is not strictly linear?

options.text: She should go back to the inspect and clean stages to investigate the suspicious value before continuing the analysis, because the workflow commonly revisits earlier stages when later stages reveal new issues.
She should continue the analysis and note the suspicious value in the final report, because the workflow always moves forward once cleaning is done.
She should restart the entire workflow from the clarify-the-question stage, because any new issue requires starting over.
She should skip the suspicious value and analyze only the remaining rows, because the workflow does not allow going back.

opt_s11_b.message: The workflow is commonly iterative, not strictly linear. When a later stage reveals a new issue, the right move is to go back to inspect or clean — not to press on and note it later.

opt_s11_c.message: The loop-back goes to inspect or clean, not all the way back to clarifying the question. Restarting from the beginning would be unnecessary and wasteful.

opt_s11_d.message: Skipping a suspicious value without investigating it would leave a quality problem unaddressed. The workflow allows — and expects — going back to inspect or clean when a new issue appears.

correct.message: Correct. The analysis workflow is commonly iterative: when a later stage reveals a new issue, you go back to inspect or clean before continuing. This is not a failure — it is the expected behaviour of a careful analyst.

incorrect.message: Think about what the workflow diagram showed: there are loop-back arrows from the analyze and visualize stages pointing back to inspect. What does that mean for what to do when you find a suspicious value?

hints: Recall what you read about the workflow being iterative rather than strictly linear — what does that mean when a suspicious value turns up during analysis?
Earlier stages such as inspecting or cleaning may be revisited when later stages reveal new issues — which stage would you return to?

correct.message: Correct. The six stages in order are: clarify the question → inspect → clean → analyze → visualize → communicate. Analyze and visualize are kept as separate steps. When a suspicious value appears during analysis, the workflow loops back to inspect (or clean) before continuing.

steps.title: The people behind the data
steps.lede: The delivery-orders table contains information about real people — that changes how you should handle it.

blocks.text: The Kwik Courier delivery-orders table almost certainly contains information about real people — customers' addresses, drivers' names. Data users should respect the privacy and confidentiality of the individuals a dataset describes, which means treating that table as more than just numbers to analyze.

Responsible data handling includes minimizing data collection to what is needed and being accountable for how the data is used — if the analysis only needs delivery times and cities, there is no reason to keep customers phone numbers. Data work should also consider its potential impact on the people and communities it affects: a finding like slow deliveries in one neighborhood could affect real customers and drivers, not just look interesting in a report.

steps.title: Honest reporting and the limits of removing names
steps.lede: Sharing findings responsibly means stating what the data can and cannot claim — and knowing that removing a name column is not enough.

blocks.text: When sharing data and findings, data users should honestly report data limitations and known biases rather than overstating certainty — if the delivery data only covers one week, or one driver logged times inconsistently, that limitation belongs in the report. Identifying information that is not needed for the purpose should be left out or removed, especially before data is shared; findings can describe a group without identifying individuals — reporting 'the eastern delivery zone runs slow' rather than naming individual customers.

Removing identifying information does not by itself remove the risk of re-identification: the data, combined with other available data, can still identify people, so removing a name column alone is not automatically enough.

steps.title: Privacy, minimal collection, and impact
steps.lede: Apply the principles of privacy, minimal collection and impact thinking to the delivery-orders scenario.

public.prompt: The analyst needs to share a summary of average delivery times per city with the operations manager. The current dataset includes order_id, order_date, city, delivery_minutes, driver_id, customer_name, and customer_phone. Which columns should she remove before sharing, and why?

options.text: She should remove customer_name and customer_phone, because identifying information that is not needed for the purpose should be left out before data is shared, and the analysis only needs delivery times and cities.
She should keep all columns, because removing data might make the analysis less complete.
She should remove driver_id as well as customer_name and customer_phone, because driver identifiers are also personal data.
She does not need to remove anything, because the operations manager is authorised to see all company data.

opt_s15_b.message: Responsible data handling means minimizing data to what is needed. Keeping customer names and phone numbers when the analysis only needs delivery times and cities is not necessary — and it exposes personal data without purpose.

opt_s15_c.message: driver_id is a numeric code, not personally identifying information about customers. The columns to remove are those that identify individual customers and are not needed for the stated purpose.

opt_s15_d.message: Authorization to access data does not remove the responsibility to minimize what is shared. Identifying information that is not needed for the purpose should be left out before sharing, regardless of who the recipient is.

correct.message: Correct. Identifying information that is not needed for the purpose — customer names and phone numbers — should be left out before sharing. The analysis only needs delivery times and cities, so there is no reason to include personal data.

incorrect.message: Think about which columns are actually needed to calculate average delivery times per city. Any column that identifies individual customers but is not needed for the analysis should be removed before sharing.

hints: Which columns does the analyst actually need to calculate average delivery time per city?
Which columns contain information that could identify individual customers?

steps.title: Honest reporting and re-identification risk
steps.lede: Recognise when a finding overstates certainty, and why removing names is not always enough.

public.prompt: The analyst removes customer_name and customer_phone from the dataset before sharing it. She also notices the data only covers one week. Which of the following best describes what she should do?

options.text: She should note in her report that the data covers only one week, because data users should honestly report limitations rather than overstating certainty. She should also be aware that removing names does not fully eliminate re-identification risk, since the remaining data combined with other sources could still identify individuals.
She has done enough by removing the name columns; the data is now fully anonymised and she can report findings without caveats.
She should not mention the one-week limitation, because it might make the findings seem less reliable to the manager.
She should delete the entire dataset after the analysis to prevent any re-identification risk.

opt_s16_b.message: Removing identifying columns does not by itself remove re-identification risk. The remaining data, combined with other available data, can still identify people. And the one-week limitation is a genuine constraint that should be reported honestly.

opt_s16_c.message: Data users should honestly report data limitations and known biases rather than overstating certainty. Hiding the one-week limitation would mislead the manager about how reliable the findings are.

opt_s16_d.message: Deleting the dataset is not the right response to re-identification risk. The right response is to be aware of the risk, minimize unnecessary data, and report limitations honestly.

correct.message: Correct. Honest reporting means stating the one-week limitation so the manager knows how far to trust the findings. And removing names does not fully eliminate re-identification risk — the remaining data combined with other sources could still identify individuals.

incorrect.message: Think about two separate responsibilities: what should be reported about the data's limitations, and what removing names does and does not achieve for privacy.

hints: If the data only covers one week, what should the analyst tell the manager about how confident to be in the findings?
Does removing a name column make data fully anonymous? What else could someone use to identify a person?

steps.title: Which columns should you keep?
steps.lede: Given the delivery-orders table and a stated analysis purpose, select the columns to keep before sharing — and note one limitation to report.

public.intro: The operations manager has asked for a report on average delivery times per city. Before sharing the dataset, you need to remove any columns that are not needed for this purpose and that could identify individual customers.

task_remove_name.correct: Correct. customer_name is personally identifiable information that is not needed to calculate average delivery times per city.

task_remove_phone.correct: Correct. customer_phone is personally identifiable information that is not needed for this analysis.

correct.message: Correct. customer_name and customer_phone are personally identifiable information not needed to calculate average delivery times per city — they must be removed before sharing. Note that removing these columns does not fully eliminate re-identification risk: the remaining data combined with other sources could still identify individuals. Also note the one-week data coverage as a limitation to state in your report.

steps.title: What you've learned
steps.lede: Three ideas that will shape every analysis you run.

blocks.text: Running completeness, uniqueness, validity and accuracy checks on the delivery-orders table before analyzing it is what tells you whether you can trust what the numbers say. The analysis workflow — clarify, inspect, clean, analyze, visualize, communicate — is commonly iterative: earlier stages may be revisited as later stages reveal new issues. Treating the people behind the data with care, and being honest about what the analysis can and cannot claim, is as much a part of the job as getting the numbers right.
